strengths: Originality/significance: Training a small open-weight model with reinforcement learning to produce instance-specific natural-language advice for a frozen black-box model is a useful extension of static prompt optimization. Transfer from inexpensive training-time students to frontier models is particularly practically relevant.

Soundness: The paper evaluates several distinct settings—RuleArena Taxes, MTOB translation, SWE-agent efficiency, and three personalization tasks—and generally includes student-only, untrained-advisor, and static-optimizer baselines. The ablations on prompt initialization, advisor family, cross-provider transfer, and direct RL help characterize the method.

Empirical promise: Several gains are substantial, including MTOB improving from 33.2 to 45.8 chrF, RuleArena from 64.8% to 76.8% with the training-time student, and large personalization gains. The observation that an untrained advisor can hurt performance usefully motivates learning the advisor.

Presentation: The high-level architecture, two-step, three-step, and multi-turn variants are explained clearly, and figures make the principal results easy to understand. The paper also candidly reports a negative MATH-500 result and that direct RL outperforms the proposed approach.
The method leaves the advised model unchanged and produces inspectable natural-language advice, potentially making deployment and diagnosis easier than weight-level adaptation.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several headline claims are broader than the evidence. “Robustness” and preservation of general capabilities are inferred only from MATH-500 accuracy for two specialized advisors; this single benchmark cannot establish that unrelated capabilities are preserved, and inference-time advice can plainly alter behavior even though the student weights are frozen.

Soundness: The frontier evaluations are small or narrow. RuleArena uses only 25 test examples, SWE-agent uses 49 issues from a single Tenacity repository, and personalization evaluates new prompts for identities already heavily represented during training. There is no evaluation on unseen users, so the results mainly demonstrate memorization of name-to-preference mappings rather than general preference inference.

Soundness/statistics: The manuscript does not adequately specify what the 95% confidence intervals average over, how stochastic API generations are handled, the number of independent training runs, or the statistical tests used. Claims such as maintaining SWE resolve rate rely on overlapping intervals rather than an equivalence/non-inferiority test; on Gemini 3 Pro the rate actually changes from 82.9% to 80.8%.

Baseline validity: Comparing a parameterized 7–8B advisor with a single static prompt gives the proposed method far greater storage and per-instance computation. Equal reward-query counts do not equalize model capacity or inference cost. Stronger dynamic baselines—retrieval of per-user profiles, supervised advice generation, per-user prompts, or test-time reflection—are missing. GEPA is omitted entirely for SWE-agent, weakening the general claim of outperforming prompt optimizers.

The personalization oracle is poorly constructed: it places every user's preference into one static prompt instead of retrieving only the relevant user's known preference. Its underperformance therefore does not convincingly show that learned advising is superior to an oracle with full information.

Reproducibility: Important details are absent, including random seeds, decoding parameters for student/evaluator calls, exact API model snapshots, full prompts for most domains, GRPO-specific settings, reward-normalization details, dataset split identities, and baseline hyperparameters. The work uses a “lightly modified” SkyRL fork without describing the modifications, while the manuscript's code link is blank.

There is an apparent configuration inconsistency: Figure 3 reports a Qwen3 8B advisor for RuleArena, whereas the frontier-transfer Figure 4 reports Qwen2.5 7B, despite the text describing this as transfer of the advisor trained with GPT-4.1 mini. This makes a central transfer result difficult to interpret or reproduce.

Significance/scope: MTOB transfer to GPT-5 is only 1.6 chrF, and the strong RuleArena transfer rests on the unexplained anomaly that GPT-5 scores dramatically below GPT-4.1 mini. The paper does not investigate whether prompting, reasoning settings, or model-version effects cause this anomaly.

Originality: Learned prompt/advice generators and RL-based prompt rewriting have substantial precedent. The per-instance, multi-turn, and cross-model formulation is valuable, but the paper does not sharply isolate which component is novel through controlled comparisons against the closest trained prompt-generator methods.

Efficiency is incompletely assessed. Training requires up to 32,000 black-box calls and eight H100 GPUs, while inference adds an advisor call—and in the three-step variant an additional student call. No measured monetary cost, latency, token usage, or quality-versus-cost analysis is provided, making “practical and cost-effective” insufficiently supported.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section chiefly notes that the advisor needs something useful to learn. It omits reward hacking, prompt injection, harmful or misleading advice, privacy implications of encoding latent user preferences, manipulation risks, evaluator-model bias, and the possibility that advice transfers undesirable behaviors. These are material for a method explicitly intended to steer black-box systems.

Presentation contains avoidable imprecision and errors, including saying SWE steps are “efficiency” and are reduced from 31.7 to 26.3, an incorrect appendix reference (“Appendix 1”), malformed or inconsistent bibliography dates/URLs, and repeated grammatical/typographic issues. These do not invalidate the idea but reduce confidence in the experimental record.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and practically motivated modular framework: a small trainable model generates instance-conditioned natural-language advice for a frozen model. The evaluation spans specialized reasoning, translation, software agents, and personalization, with useful ablations on initialization, cross-family transfer, advisor backbones, and direct RL.

Several empirical results are promising, particularly the MTOB improvement from 33.2 to 45.8 chrF and the maintenance of SWE-agent resolve rate while reducing interaction steps for the training-time student.
Natural-language advice is interpretable, and the examples suggest that training can replace vague guidance with more actionable, task-specific instructions.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not statistically robust enough for the breadth of the claims. RuleArena uses only 25 test examples, SWE uses 49 issues from one repository, and MTOB uses 50 examples. The paper reports 95% intervals and isolated p-values without defining their computation, the number of evaluation samples, random seeds, or whether variation across training runs was measured. Apparently single-run results cannot establish reliable RL improvements or transfer.

The frontier-model comparisons omit critical controls. Figures 4 and 6 compare a trained-advisor pipeline against the frontier student alone, but generally omit an untrained advisor, matched static advice, self-revision, and GEPA/PAG evaluated with that same frontier model and inference budget. This is particularly problematic for the three-step tax pipeline, which grants extra generation and revision calls. Consequently, the results do not isolate learning in the advisor from added inference-time computation or generic critique effects.

The personalization experiments largely test memorization and routing among recurring user identifiers. Training and evaluation contain the same five—or, in the scaling experiment, the same 100—users, with many training observations per user. The paper does not evaluate unseen users, preference changes, sparse histories, or noisy feedback. Moreover, the purported in-context oracle places every user's preferences into one prompt instead of supplying the relevant user's known preference directly. Beating this overloaded oracle therefore does not demonstrate learning beyond full information; it mainly demonstrates effective retrieval/routing under an artificially disadvantaged baseline.

The robustness claim is substantially overstated. Capability retention is tested only on MATH-500 using two personalized pipelines; one advised result is numerically lower than baseline (0.634 versus 0.660). Failure to detect a difference on one benchmark is not evidence of “no degradation on other benchmarks,” especially since the paper itself shows that an untrained advisor can sharply harm RuleArena performance. Freezing student weights prevents parameter forgetting but does not ensure that injected advice is behaviorally harmless.

The headline SWE claim is internally inconsistent: reducing Gemini 3 Pro from 31.7 to 26.3 steps is approximately 17.0%, not 24.6%. The reported 24.6% corresponds instead to Gemini 2.5 Flash decreasing from 19.1 to 14.4 steps. This undermines confidence in the abstract's quantitative summary.

Originality is limited relative to Directional Stimulus Prompting, PRewrite, Black-Box Prompt Optimization, and Matryoshka Pilot, all of which train auxiliary mechanisms to steer frozen models. Removing supervised initialization, allowing unconstrained advice, and broadening the empirical scope may be useful, but the manuscript does not sharply formalize what is technically new enough to support its “new paradigm” framing.

The cost-effectiveness claim is not demonstrated. Training uses eight H100 GPUs, many epochs, and large numbers of API calls, while three-step inference can require two student calls plus an advisor call. There is no measured dollar cost, token usage, latency, compute-normalized comparison, or inference-cost analysis. Matching GEPA only by reward-function accesses does not establish comparable total resources.

Reproducibility is inadequate. “Code available at:” is left blank; the implementation is described only as a lightly modified SkyRL fork. Exact data splits, seeds, most domain prompts, judge prompts, GRPO parameters, decoding settings for student models, confidence-interval procedure, GEPA/PAG configurations, model snapshots, and API evaluation dates are absent. Results involving mutable proprietary APIs will therefore be especially difficult to reproduce.

Limitations and ethics are treated narrowly. The paper acknowledges the need for learnable signal but does not adequately discuss reward hacking, malicious or prompt-injected advice, privacy implications of encoding user-specific preferences in model weights, conflicting preferences, biased LLM judges, or deployment safeguards. These concerns are material for a proposed black-box personalization and steering mechanism.

strengths: Originality: The paper presents a compelling formulation of black-box adaptation: a trainable open-weight model generates instance-specific natural-language advice and is optimized using only downstream rewards. Although related to learned prompt generators and directional prompting, combining per-instance advice, reinforcement learning, multi-turn advising, and transfer between student models is a meaningful contribution.

Soundness: The method is evaluated across substantially different settings—tax reasoning, low-resource translation, software engineering, and personalization—and generally improves both the training-time student and stronger frontier models. Particularly notable results include GPT-5 improving from 31.2% to 53.6% on RuleArena Taxes and GPT-4o mini improving from 33.2 to 45.8 chrF on MTOB.

Significance: Transferring an advisor trained with an inexpensive API model to GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude models addresses an important practical constraint. Cross-provider transfer and the Llama-advisor ablation suggest the mechanism is not narrowly tied to one model family.

The comparisons with untrained advisors are informative: they show that adding advice can actively harm performance and that reinforcement learning—not merely inserting another model—is responsible for much of the improvement. The comparison with direct RL also appropriately demonstrates that advising is useful but does not supersede weight-level optimization when weights are available.

Presentation: The central architecture, two-step/three-step variants, and multi-turn construction are clearly explained. The paper includes useful qualitative advice examples, prompt-initialization analysis, capability-retention checks, and an honest negative result on MATH-500.

Reproducibility is partially supported by reporting data splits, principal model configurations, reward definitions, epochs, hardware, and several training hyperparameters. The paper also identifies meaningful limitations, including inference overhead for the three-step variant, high-variance rewards, weaker gains when the student already knows the domain, and direct RL's superior performance.
weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest comparisons are not compute-matched at inference. The three-step RuleArena system uses two student calls plus an advisor call, whereas the principal student-only baseline uses one student call. More generally, the learned system adds a 7B–8B model and additional tokens. Comparisons against self-reflection, repeated sampling, a verifier/cascade, or another dynamic inference-time method under matched calls, tokens, latency, and cost are needed to isolate the benefit of advisor training.

The SWE efficiency claim counts only student-environment interactions and excludes advisor inference. Because advice is generated every five student actions, fewer environment steps need not imply lower wall-clock time, token use, or monetary cost. There is also a numerical inconsistency: Gemini 3 Pro decreases from 31.7 to 26.3 steps, about 17.0%, not the 24.6% reduction attributed to Gemini 3 Pro in the abstract; 24.6% corresponds approximately to the Gemini 2.5 Flash result (19.1 to 14.4).

The evidence appears to come from single RL training runs. The reported 95% intervals quantify evaluation uncertainty but do not capture training-seed variance, which can be substantial for GRPO on small datasets such as the 56-task SWE training set and 75-example RuleArena split. Exact interval construction and statistical tests are mostly unspecified.

The personalization tasks largely test memorization of a small mapping from user names to synthetic latent attributes: five users in the main review experiments and four preference combinations in Math Solutions. A direct per-user lookup/profile learned from rewards, a retrieved user history, and an oracle containing only the relevant user's preference would be more diagnostic baselines. Supplying the oracle with every user's preferences unnecessarily burdens the static baseline, weakening the claim that the learned advisor surpasses full-information prompting.

The broad robustness claim is insufficiently supported. Capability retention is tested only on MATH-500 for two personalization-trained advisors, with non-significant point differences. This does not establish that advisors cause 'no degradation on other benchmarks,' since harmful or irrelevant advice could affect other capabilities and distributions even though the underlying student weights remain unchanged.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: most task-specific advisor/student prompts are absent, as are exact sampled example identifiers or split seeds, decoding settings for black-box models, detailed GRPO configuration, checkpoint-selection rules, API model snapshots, training seeds, and the procedure used to compute confidence intervals. The manuscript's code-availability line is blank in the supplied version.

Presentation is generally strong, but several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, including 'static methods fail entirely,' 'near-perfect learning' as a general personalization result, and inference that transferred improvements prove advice is interpretable. The qualitative examples are suggestive but do not constitute a systematic interpretability analysis.

Ethics and limitations: The technical limitations discussion is welcome and should not be penalized, but the paper lacks discussion of privacy risks from encoding user-specific preferences in model weights, malicious or unsafe advice, prompt injection through user/environment text, and whether advising can bypass safeguards of proprietary student models. These issues are material for a proposed personalization and black-box steering mechanism.
